subject: science

items.q: Which of these shows a chemical property of an element?
items.correct: Magnesium burning brightly in air
items.misconception: Gallium melting in a person's hand
items.why: A melted solid looks very different, so it seems to have become something new. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reviews research in which students thought changes of state were chemical reactions, and lists this among the key difficulties. Ask: is a new substance made? Melted gallium is still gallium, and it turns solid again when it cools. Only a reaction, such as burning, shows a chemical property.
items.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements
items.random_wrong: Iodine crystals dissolving in ethanol

items.q: Chlorine is a gas, bromine a liquid and iodine a solid at room temperature. All three are in Group 7. What does this show?
items.correct: Elements in one group can be in different states
items.misconception: These three cannot really all be in one group
items.why: Students learn that a group is a 'family' of elements with similar properties and take 'similar' to mean 'the same'. It is a common error teachers see. Similar is not identical. Look for the trend going down a group: a steady change in melting point, state or reactivity.
items.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements
items.random_wrong: Their single atoms are a gas, a liquid and a solid

items.q: The chart shows the melting points of four metals. Which statement does the chart support?
items.correct: Two of these metals melt below 100 °C
items.misconception: All four of these metals are solids at 20 °C
items.why: Almost every metal students handle is solid, and 'metal' suggests something hard. It is a common error teachers see. Mercury is the exception: it is shiny, conducts electricity and is a metal, but it is a liquid at 20 °C.
items.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements
items.random_wrong: Each of these metals has a high melting point

items.q: How did Mendeleev put the elements in order in his table?
items.correct: By atomic mass, keeping similar elements together
items.misconception: By atomic number, as today's table does
items.why: Today's table is ordered by atomic number, and students assume that scientists in 1869 knew what we know now. Oak National Academy's lesson 'Development of the periodic table' lists as a common misconception that pupils believe scientists already knew about the particles inside atoms when the table was devised; that this leads pupils to think Mendeleev used atomic number is our inference. Mendeleev ordered the elements by atomic mass and moved some where needed to keep similar elements together. Atomic number came later.
items.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
items.random_wrong: By atomic mass alone, with no swaps made

items.q: The diagram shows part of the periodic table with today's atomic masses. Mendeleev put tellurium (Te) before iodine (I). Why?
items.correct: To put iodine with chlorine and bromine
items.misconception: He had misread the two atomic masses
items.why: Students are told the table was ordered by atomic mass and apply the rule strictly. It is a common error teachers see. For Mendeleev, properties came first: atomic mass set the rough order, and similar properties decided each element's group.
items.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
items.random_wrong: He was ordering by atomic number

items.q: Mendeleev left a gap in the group with silicon and tin. What did he expect the missing element to be like?
items.correct: Similar to silicon and tin in its group
items.misconception: Like the elements on either side in its row
items.why: Things placed side by side in everyday lists are usually alike, and students may also mix up the words group and period. It is a common error teachers see. Look down a column for similar elements. Across a row, elements change from metals to non-metals.
items.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
items.random_wrong: Identical to silicon and tin in every way

items.q: Argon, the first noble gas to be collected, was found in 1894. Where were the noble gases in Mendeleev's first table, made in 1869?
items.correct: Nowhere: his table had no place for them
items.misconception: In Group 0, just as in today's table
items.why: Students meet one finished table and do not see its history. In an RSC Education article on teaching the history of the periodic table, Peter Banks writes that it is common for students to think the table has remained unchanged since the 1800s. Scientific models change as new evidence arrives. Argon, the first noble gas to be collected, was found in 1894, after Mendeleev's first table, and the noble gases needed a new group.
items.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
items.random_wrong: In the gaps he had left for them

items.q: In the periodic table, what is a period?
items.correct: A row of elements going across the table
items.misconception: A column of elements down the table
items.why: Both words are new to students, and nothing in everyday language links 'group' to a column, so the two are easily swapped. It is a common error teachers see. Groups go down, like a family tree; periods go across, like a line of writing.
items.specStatementText: the periodic table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals
items.random_wrong: A family of elements that react alike

items.q: The diagram shows an outline of the periodic table with one column shaded. Which statement about the shaded elements is correct?
items.correct: They all react in a similar way
items.misconception: They are all gases at room temperature
items.why: The non-metals students hear about most in everyday life, such as oxygen, nitrogen and hydrogen, are gases. It is a common error teachers see. Check each element: Group 7 alone has gases (fluorine, chlorine), a liquid (bromine) and a solid (iodine).
items.specStatementText: the periodic table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals
items.random_wrong: They form one period of the table

The whole column numbered 7, from the second row to the sixth, is shaded; all the shaded boxes are to the right of the staircase line.

items.q: What does the staircase line on the periodic table separate?
items.correct: Metal elements from non-metals
items.misconception: Reactive elements from unreactive ones
items.why: The most dramatic reactions students see are reactive metals such as sodium and potassium in water. The RSC Education article 'How to teach non-metals' (Education in Chemistry) says students tend to think of the explosions of reactive metals and are usually surprised to find that fluorine, a non-metal, is the most reactive element. That this leads students to think non-metals do not burn, or that the staircase line separates reactive from unreactive elements, is our inference. Reactivity is not a metal-only property: the halogens are reactive non-metals, and the noble gases are unreactive non-metals.
items.specStatementText: the periodic table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals
items.random_wrong: Solid elements from gaseous ones

items.q: Potassium is below sodium in Group 1. Bromine is below chlorine in Group 7. Compared with the element above it, how reactive is each?
items.correct: Potassium more; bromine less
items.misconception: Potassium more; bromine more
items.why: Group 1 is usually taught first, with dramatic demonstrations, and its trend is then applied to every group. It is a common error teachers see. Learn each group's trend separately: Group 1 gets more reactive going down; Group 7 gets less reactive going down.
items.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
items.random_wrong: Potassium less; bromine less

items.q: Rubidium is just below potassium in Group 1. How will rubidium react with water, compared with potassium?
items.correct: More vigorously, as it is lower in the group
items.misconception: Less vigorously, as the top one reacts most
items.why: Students apply the Group 7 trend to every group, or assume that the first or lightest element must react most. It is a common error teachers see. Check which group it is: going down Group 1 reactivity rises; going down Group 7 it falls.
items.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
items.random_wrong: Just as vigorously, as it is in one group

items.q: The diagram shows how hot iron wool reacts with three Group 7 elements. Fluorine is above chlorine. Predict how hot iron wool reacts with fluorine.
items.correct: Even more strongly than with chlorine
items.misconception: Nothing can be said without a test
items.why: Students are taught that science needs experiments and may not see that a prediction comes before the test. It is a common error teachers see. A prediction uses a pattern; a test checks it. Mendeleev predicted germanium's properties 15 years before it was found.
items.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
items.random_wrong: Less strongly than it does with iodine

items.q: Sodium burns in chlorine. Xenon is in Group 0, below krypton. Predict what happens when sodium is heated in xenon.
items.correct: No reaction, as xenon is a noble gas
items.misconception: It burns, as xenon is a gas like chlorine
items.why: Shine is the first thing students notice about metals. The RSC Education article 'How to teach non-metals' (Education in Chemistry) notes that students may use a single property to classify an element and that a shiny lump of graphite may be mistaken for a metal; treating the state of an element (for example, being a gas) as enough to predict its reactions is our extension of the same habit. Weigh up several properties together, and check the element's position: to the right of the staircase line means a non-metal.
items.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
items.random_wrong: It reacts, as xenon is low in its group

items.q: Which property do all metals have?
items.correct: They can conduct electricity
items.misconception: They are attracted to a magnet
items.why: Many everyday metal objects, such as steel cans and paper clips, stick to magnets. IOP Spark's research review of misconceptions lists that many students expect all metals to be attracted by magnets. Being attracted to a magnet is a property of only a few metals; use conductivity, shine and position in the table to identify a metal.
items.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals
items.random_wrong: They are solid at room temperature

items.q: The table shows some properties of four elements. Which conclusion does the table support?
items.correct: A non-metal can still conduct electricity
items.misconception: Carbon must be a metal, as it conducts
items.why: Primary-school sorting activities put metal conductors against non-metal insulators. IOP Spark notes that teaching materials classify metals as conductors and non-metals as insulators, and the RSC Education article 'How to teach non-metals' says students often treat metals and non-metals as completely opposite in their properties. Typical properties have exceptions: graphite is a non-metal that conducts, and mercury is a metal that is liquid.
items.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals
items.random_wrong: Iodine is a metal, as it is shiny

items.q: Sodium is soft enough to cut with a knife and melts at 98 °C. Is sodium a metal?
items.correct: Yes: it is one of the alkali metals
items.misconception: Yes: each sodium atom is soft and shiny
items.why: Students picture atoms as tiny pieces of the substance they can see, so they give each atom the substance's properties. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports Ben-Zvi and colleagues' finding that nearly half of 15-year-olds gave single copper atoms the bulk properties of copper, and the RSC diagnostic probe 'Iron – a metal: true or false?' (Taber, 2002) targets the same idea, for example that iron is hard because iron atoms are hard. Keep two levels apart: what you see and measure belongs to a piece of the element; atoms are the tiny particles it is made of.
items.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals
items.random_wrong: No: metals are hard and difficult to melt

items.q: Sodium oxide and calcium oxide are metal oxides that dissolve in water. What do they form?
items.correct: An alkaline solution
items.misconception: An acidic solution
items.why: Students know that acids react with metals and so link 'metal' with 'acid'; others remember the rule back to front. It is a common error teachers see. Link the oxide to its element: sodium and calcium are metals, and their oxides make alkalis; sulfur is a non-metal, and its oxide helps make acid rain.
items.specStatementText: the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity
items.random_wrong: Just a neutral solution

items.q: Element X burns in oxygen. Its oxide dissolves in water, making a solution of pH 3. What is X most likely to be?
items.correct: A non-metal, as its oxide is acidic
items.misconception: Either, as all oxides are acidic
items.why: The oxides students hear about most are carbon dioxide in fizzy drinks and sulfur dioxide in acid rain, and both are acidic. It is a common error teachers see. Ask what the oxide is made from: the oxide of a metal such as sodium is a base; the oxide of a non-metal such as sulfur is acidic.
items.specStatementText: the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity
items.random_wrong: A metal, since metal oxides are acidic

items.q: Copper oxide powder is stirred with water and filtered. The filtered water has pH 7. What is copper oxide?
items.correct: A base, as it can neutralise acids
items.misconception: A neutral oxide, as the water is pH 7
items.why: Students use the indicator test as the only test, and an oxide that does not dissolve leaves water at pH 7. It is a common error teachers see. Indicator only shows what has dissolved. To find out whether an insoluble oxide is a base, see whether it neutralises an acid.
items.specStatementText: the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity
items.random_wrong: An acidic oxide, like any oxide

items.q: Element W is dull and grey. It conducts electricity, a magnet does not attract it, and it can be hammered flat. What is W?
items.correct: A metal, as it is malleable and conducts
items.misconception: A metal, as only metals conduct electricity
items.why: Primary-school sorting activities put metal conductors against non-metal insulators. IOP Spark notes that teaching materials classify metals as conductors and non-metals as insulators, and the RSC Education article 'How to teach non-metals' says students often treat metals and non-metals as completely opposite in their properties. Typical properties have exceptions: graphite is a non-metal that conducts, and mercury is a metal that is liquid.
items.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals
items.random_wrong: A non-metal, as it is dull, not shiny

items.q: When iodine dissolves in ethanol, is a new substance made?
items.correct: No. Dissolving is a physical change: the iodine spreads out through the ethanol, and evaporating the ethanol gives the iodine back.
items.misconception: Dissolving is a chemical change: the substance that dissolves is turned into something new.
items.why: The solid seems to vanish and the liquid often changes colour. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports Schollum's finding that about half of 14- and 16-year-olds thought sugar dissolving was a chemical change. Dissolving makes a mixture (a solution), not a new substance. The dissolved substance can be got back by evaporating the solvent.
items.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Does stirring iron filings and sulfur powder together make a new substance?
items.correct: No. Stirring only mixes them, and each keeps its own properties: a magnet can still pull out the iron. A new substance, iron sulfide, forms only when the mixture is heated and reacts.
items.misconception: Mixing two elements together makes a new substance, so mixing is a chemical change.
items.why: In cooking and everyday life, mixing things 'makes' something new, and a mixture can look different from the substances in it. It is a common error teachers see. Check whether the parts keep their properties. If they can be separated by a physical method, such as a magnet, they were only mixed.
items.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Did Mendeleev leave gaps, or swap elements, to make his table look neat?
items.correct: No. His choices followed the properties of the elements: gaps were left for elements not yet discovered, and some elements were swapped so each one sat with elements like it.
items.misconception: Mendeleev's gaps and swaps were there to make his table look neat and even.
items.why: Tables in everyday life are tidied to look even, and the gaps look like spaces left for layout. It is a common error teachers see. Each gap was a prediction: an element should exist there, with properties like the elements above and below it.
items.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is the periodic table a list of elements in order of reactivity?
items.correct: No. The periodic table orders the elements by atomic number (Mendeleev used atomic mass) and puts similar elements in the same column. The reactivity series is a different list.
items.misconception: The periodic table lists the elements in order of how reactive they are.
items.why: Students meet the reactivity series and the periodic table in the same years, and both are lists of elements in an order. It is a common error teachers see. Keep the two apart: the reactivity series ranks metals by reactivity; the periodic table orders elements by atomic number and lines up similar ones in groups.
items.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Did Mendeleev leave a gap for every element discovered after 1869?
items.correct: No. He left gaps only where his pattern showed that an element was missing. He did not know that a whole group, the noble gases, was missing, so his first table had no place for them.
items.misconception: Mendeleev left gaps for all the undiscovered elements, including the noble gases.
items.why: Students learn that the gaps were later filled by new elements and assume every later element went into one of them. It is a common error teachers see. Only a few elements, such as gallium, scandium and germanium, filled Mendeleev's gaps. The noble gases needed a new column.
items.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Which way do the reactivity trends in Groups 1 and 7 go?
items.correct: Going down Group 1, the metals get more reactive. Going down Group 7, the halogens get less reactive.
items.misconception: Reactivity falls going down Group 1 and rises going down Group 7: the two trends are swapped.
items.why: Students remember that the two groups have opposite trends but not which way each one goes. It is a common error teachers see. Anchor each trend with an example: potassium bursts into flames on water while lithium only fizzes; chlorine reacts more strongly than iodine.
items.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Are all metals hard, with high melting points?
items.correct: No. Most are, but sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a knife and melt below 100 °C, and mercury melts at −39 °C.
items.misconception: All metals are hard and have high melting points.
items.why: The metals students know best, such as iron, steel and copper, are hard and melt only at very high temperatures. It is a common error teachers see. Treat typical properties as a guide, not a rule: the Group 1 metals are soft and melt at low temperatures.
items.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Does a metal oxide give off hydrogen when it reacts with water, as the metal does?
items.correct: No. Sodium gives off hydrogen with water, but sodium oxide does not: sodium oxide + water → sodium hydroxide, an alkaline solution.
items.misconception: A metal oxide reacts with water in the same way as the metal itself, giving off hydrogen.
items.why: Students have just learned that Group 1 metals fizz in water, making hydrogen and an alkali, and apply the same reaction to the metal's oxide. It is a common error teachers see. Compare the word equations: sodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen, but sodium oxide + water → sodium hydroxide only.

items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is every metal oxide an alkali?
items.correct: No. Copper oxide is a base (it neutralises acids) but it does not dissolve in water, so it is not an alkali. An alkali is a base that dissolves, such as sodium oxide.
items.misconception: 'Base' and 'alkali' mean the same thing, so every metal oxide is an alkali.
items.why: The two words are often used loosely as if they meant the same, and the metal oxides students test first do dissolve to make alkalis. It is a common error teachers see. Every alkali is a base, but not every base is an alkali: an alkali is a base that dissolves in water.
